subject: Statistics 1 · Foundation
title: Describing numerical data
description: Read numerical distributions, calculate center and spread, and understand both course percentile methods.

intro.text: Read numerical distributions, calculate center and spread, and understand both course percentile methods.

sections.title: Numerical frequency tables: values and intervals

blocks.text: A numerical variable records an amount, such as household size, height, or marks. Before finding an average, organize the numbers so you can see which values occur often.

blocks.alt: Count distinct values for discrete data, or use non-overlapping intervals for measurements.
blocks.caption: Count distinct values for discrete data, or use non-overlapping intervals for measurements.

blocks.text: Discrete counts and continuous measurements

A discrete variable usually counts things: 1, 2 or 3 people in a household. A continuous variable usually measures things: height might be 162.4 cm. Recorded measurements are often rounded, but the quantity itself can still be continuous. Large sets of discrete values can also be grouped into intervals.
Worked example: household sizes
The lecture gives 15 responses: 2,1,3,4,5,2,3,3,3,4,4,1,2,3,4. List each distinct value, count it, then divide by 15 to find its relative frequency.
Group many values into classes

A class, bin, or interval is a range of values. For example, [40,50) includes 40 and all values below 50, but excludes 50. The next class [50,60) includes 50. This left-in, right-out rule ensures that boundary values are counted once.

For half-open continuous intervals there is no greatest included real number below 50. Think of 50 as the upper boundary, rather than an included maximum. If an exercise uses inclusive integer limits such as 40–49, read that convention carefully.
Worked example: the lecture’s grouped marks table

Source clarification: the printed raw marks list contains 49 numbers, while the grouped table totals 50. Counting that printed list gives 17 in [50,60), not 18. Here we label the 50-case grouped table as given; we do not invent a missing observation. Use the stated grouped table when a question supplies it.
Choose sensible classes

The lecture suggests roughly 5–20 classes as a starting point, not a law. Too few bins hide detail; too many make the picture noisy. Cover every observation, avoid overlap, and normally use equal widths. Keep the bins in numerical order.

blocks.question: Which class contains 60: [50,60) or [60,70)?
blocks.answer: [60,70). Its left endpoint is included; the earlier class excludes its right endpoint.
blocks.text: Which class contains 60: [50,60) or [60,70)? Answer: [60,70). Its left endpoint is included; the earlier class excludes its right endpoint.

blocks.question: Data are 1,2,2,3,3,3. Give the frequency and relative frequency for 3.
blocks.answer: Frequency = 3. Relative frequency = 3/6 = 0.5 = 50%.
blocks.text: Data are 1,2,2,3,3,3. Give the frequency and relative frequency for 3. Answer: Frequency = 3. Relative frequency = 3/6 = 0.5 = 50%.

blocks.question: What is the midpoint of [20,30)?
blocks.answer: (20 + 30)/2 = 25. The midpoint is a representative value, not necessarily an observed value.
blocks.text: What is the midpoint of [20,30)? Answer: (20 + 30)/2 = 25. The midpoint is a representative value, not necessarily an observed value.

A graph helps you see where numerical observations cluster, how spread out they are, and whether there are unusual values. Two useful choices are a histogram and a stem-and-leaf plot.

blocks.alt: Equal-width numerical intervals touch; their heights show the lecture’s grouped frequencies.
blocks.caption: Equal-width numerical intervals touch; their heights show the lecture’s grouped frequencies.

blocks.text: Build a histogram step by step

First make a frequency table. Put the numerical class boundaries on the horizontal axis. Put frequency or relative frequency on the vertical axis. For each equal-width interval, draw a bar whose height is its count or share. Adjacent intervals touch, and the intervals stay in numerical order.

In the lecture table the tallest bin is [50,60), with 18 of 50 cases. Together, [50,60) and [60,70) contain 35/50 = 70% of the cases. The graph does not tell you how many students scored exactly 55, because exact positions inside a bin have been lost.
Histogram versus bar chart

rows: Equal bar widths let lengths compare counts.

blocks.text: The lecture’s count-height rule assumes equal-width classes. With unequal widths, use frequency density = frequency / class width so the bar AREA represents the count. A width-20 bin with 10 cases has density 0.5; a width-10 bin with 10 cases has density 1. They have the same area, despite different heights.
Read a numerical distribution

Look for the center, spread, shape and unusual values. A long tail toward large values is right-skewed; a long tail toward small values is left-skewed. A roughly balanced shape is symmetric. Check whether there is one main peak, more than one peak, gaps, or isolated values. Changing the bin width can change the apparent shape.
A stem-and-leaf plot keeps the original values

blocks.alt: The hospital ages are split into tens as stems and ones as leaves, with a key of 2 | 3 = 23 years.
blocks.caption: The hospital ages are split into tens as stems and ones as leaves, with a key of 2 | 3 = 23 years.

blocks.text: Use the lecture ages 15,22,29,36,31,23,45,10,25,28,48. Write stems 1,2,3,4 from smallest to largest. Put the ones digits beside the matching stem, then sort leaves within each row. There are 11 leaves for 11 observations.

Keep repeated leaves: ages 22,22,29 need stem 2 with leaves 2,2,9. Include a key so the scale is clear. With decimal data, a key such as 2 | 3 = 2.3 would mean something different. A stemplot suits small datasets; very large datasets can become crowded.

blocks.question: The bar for [60,70) has height 17. Does this mean 17 students scored 65?
blocks.answer: No. It means 17 observations fall from 60 inclusive to 70 exclusive. Their exact marks are unknown from that bar.
blocks.text: The bar for [60,70) has height 17. Does this mean 17 students scored 65? Answer: No. It means 17 observations fall from 60 inclusive to 70 exclusive. Their exact marks are unknown from that bar.

blocks.question: With key 7 | 5 = 75, what do stem 8 and leaves 0,2,2 mean?
blocks.answer: The observations are 80,82,82. Repeated leaves represent repeated observations.
blocks.text: With key 7 | 5 = 75, what do stem 8 and leaves 0,2,2 mean? Answer: The observations are 80,82,82. Repeated leaves represent repeated observations.

blocks.question: Two unequal-width bins both contain 12 cases. Must their histogram heights match?
blocks.answer: No. For an area-correct histogram, the wider bin has a lower frequency density. Their bar areas match.
blocks.text: Two unequal-width bins both contain 12 cases. Must their histogram heights match? Answer: No. For an area-correct histogram, the wider bin has a lower frequency density. Their bar areas match.

The mean is the total shared equally across all observations. It is often called the average. A measure of center tells us a typical location; it does not tell us the whole spread.

blocks.alt: Add the observations, count them, then divide. An extreme value can pull the mean.
blocks.caption: Add the observations, count them, then divide. An extreme value can pull the mean.

blocks.text: The symbols in plain English

x-bar is the sample mean, and n is the number of observations in the sample. Mu is the population mean, and N is the population size. The big sigma symbol means “add all these terms”. The same arithmetic works for measured values as well as counts.
Worked examples from the lecture
The mean need not appear in the data. For 1 and 2 children the mean is 1.5 children; it describes the average, not a possible half-child household. Large unusual values can move it strongly.
Mean from a single-value frequency table
Multiply each value by how often it occurs. Add those products. Divide by the total number of cases, not by the number of distinct values.
The household mean is 44/15 ≈ 2.933 people. Averaging 1,2,3,4,5 without frequencies would wrongly give every size the same weight.
Approximate mean from interval groups
When only intervals are known, replace every value in a class by its midpoint. This loses within-class detail, so the result is an estimate.
Estimated mean = 2940/50 = 58.8 marks. This belongs to the lecture’s 50-case grouped table; it is not an exact mean of the inconsistent 49-value printed list.
Change every value: what happens to the mean?

Adding 5 marks to each of the ten marks increases the mean from 59 to 64. Multiplying every mark by 0.4 changes the mean to 0.4 × 59 = 23.6. Multiplying by 0.4 means keeping 40% of the original, or reducing it by 60%; reducing by 40% would mean multiplying by 0.6.

blocks.question: A value 10 occurs twice and 20 occurs three times. Find the mean.
blocks.text: A value 10 occurs twice and 20 occurs three times. Find the mean. Answer: Total = 2×10 + 3×20 = 80; count = 5; mean = 80/5 = 16.

blocks.question: Two classes have frequencies 3 and 1 and midpoints 5 and 15. Estimate the mean.
blocks.answer: (3×5 + 1×15)/(3+1) = 30/4 = 7.5. This is a midpoint estimate.
blocks.text: Two classes have frequencies 3 and 1 and midpoints 5 and 15. Estimate the mean. Answer: (3×5 + 1×15)/(3+1) = 30/4 = 7.5. This is a midpoint estimate.

blocks.question: A mean is 12. Every value is multiplied by 3 then increased by 2. New mean?
blocks.text: A mean is 12. Every value is multiplied by 3 then increased by 2. New mean? Answer: 3×12 + 2 = 38.
Source: Lecture 3.2. Extra examples and diagrams are teaching material prepared for these notes.

sections.title: Numerical median, mode and choosing a center

blocks.text: The median is the middle after sorting. The mode is the most frequent value. They answer different questions from the mean, and an unusual value affects them differently.

blocks.alt: For odd n, choose the middle observation; for even n, average the two numerical middle values.
blocks.caption: For odd n, choose the middle observation; for even n, average the two numerical middle values.

blocks.text: Odd number of observations
Sort 2,12,5,7,6,7,3 to get 2,3,5,6,7,7,12. With n = 7, the middle position is (7+1)/2 = 4. The 4th value is 6, so the median is 6. The position 4 is not the median value.
Even number of observations

Sort 2,105,5,7,6,3 to get 2,3,5,6,7,105. With n = 6, middle positions are 3 and 4. Their values are 5 and 6, so the median is (5+6)/2 = 5.5. This averaging is for numerical values; it is not a rule for averaging category codes.
The mode counts repetitions

For 2,12,5,7,6,7,3, the mode is 7 because it appears twice. Changing 12 to 105 leaves mode 7. Removing one 7 leaves all values distinct; the lecture convention calls this no mode. If two repeated values tie at the highest frequency, give both modes.
Compare mean and median when an outlier changes

The median resists an extreme change because it depends on middle positions. “Resistant” does not mean it can never change. The mean includes the size of every value, so outliers can pull it toward a tail.
One complete ten-mark example
The marks sort to 35,38,47,58,61,66,68,68,70,79. Mean = 59. Median = (61+66)/2 = 63.5. Mode = 68. All three are correct summaries, but they describe different aspects of the same data.
Adding or multiplying a constant

Adding 5 to every mark adds 5 to the mean, median and each mode: they become 64,68.5,73. Multiplying every mark by 0.4 gives 23.6,25.4,27.2. Nonzero scaling preserves repetition counts; if you multiply everything by zero, all observations collapse to zero.

The median also transforms correctly for negative multipliers, although the sorted order reverses. For a mode, a nonzero transformation carries each modal value to its transformed value. A dataset with no repeated values still has no mode under the lecture convention.
Choose a summary for the question

rows: Numerical data with an extreme high income
Median often describes a typical person better.
Need the total per observation, such as average cost
Want the most common shoe size
Mode; no numerical mean or median.

blocks.question: For 3,8,8,9,20, find mean, median and mode.
blocks.answer: Mean = 48/5 = 9.6. Median = 8 (3rd value). Mode = 8 (twice).
blocks.text: For 3,8,8,9,20, find mean, median and mode. Answer: Mean = 48/5 = 9.6. Median = 8 (3rd value). Mode = 8 (twice).

blocks.question: For 1,2,2,4,4,9, find median and modes.
blocks.answer: Median = (2+4)/2 = 3. Modes = 2 and 4, each appearing twice.
blocks.text: For 1,2,2,4,4,9, find median and modes. Answer: Median = (2+4)/2 = 3. Modes = 2 and 4, each appearing twice.

blocks.question: A median is 10. Each value becomes 5 − 2x. What is the new median?
blocks.answer: 5 − 2×10 = −15. Sort order reverses, but the transformed median follows the same linear rule.
blocks.text: A median is 10. Each value becomes 5 − 2x. What is the new median? Answer: 5 − 2×10 = −15. Sort order reverses, but the transformed median follows the same linear rule.

sections.title: Spread: range, variance and standard deviation

blocks.text: Two groups can have the same mean but feel very different. Spread tells us whether values stay close together or vary widely.

blocks.alt: Both groups have mean 3, but only the second group varies.
blocks.caption: Both groups have mean 3, but only the second group varies.

blocks.text: Range: largest minus smallest
For 3,3,3,3,3, range = 3−3 = 0. For 1,2,3,4,5, range = 5−1 = 4. Replacing the last value by 15 increases the range to 15−1 = 14. Range is easy to calculate but only uses the extremes.
Why not simply add deviations?

A deviation is a value minus its mean. Positive and negative deviations cancel: for 2,4,6 with mean 4, deviations are −2,0,2, whose sum is zero. Zero total deviation does not mean zero spread. Squaring makes all contributions nonnegative.

blocks.alt: For 2,4,6, squared deviations total 8; divide by 3 for population variance or 2 for sample variance.
blocks.caption: For 2,4,6, squared deviations total 8; divide by 3 for population variance or 2 for sample variance.

blocks.text: Population variance versus sample variance

Use N when describing the whole population as given. The course uses n−1 for sample variance when the data are a sample. Sample variance needs at least two observations. After estimating the sample mean, the deviations have to sum to zero, so one deviation is fixed by the others; this helps explain the n−1 correction.
Worked example: the ten marks
Population variance = 1898/10 = 189.8 marks². Sample variance = 1898/9 ≈ 210.889 marks². The dataset is the same; the denominator depends on the requested interpretation.
Source correction: the slide writes the deviation of 66 as −7. It is +7 because 66−59 = 7. Its square is still 49, so the displayed squared-deviation total 1898 remains correct.
Standard deviation returns to the original unit

Population SD = √189.8 ≈ 13.777 marks. Sample SD = √(1898/9) ≈ 14.522 marks. If the measurements were kilograms, variance would be kg² and standard deviation would be kg. Standard deviation is a measure of spread around the mean, not a statement that every observation lies exactly that far away.
What happens when every value changes?
For the marks multiplied by 0.4, sample variance = 0.16 × (1898/9) ≈ 33.7422 and sample SD ≈ 5.8088. Adding a constant shifts every point and its mean together, so distances do not change.

blocks.question: For the population 1,3,5, find range, variance and SD.
blocks.answer: Mean = 3. Range = 4. Squared deviations are 4,0,4; population variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.667 and SD ≈ 1.633.
blocks.text: For the population 1,3,5, find range, variance and SD. Answer: Mean = 3. Range = 4. Squared deviations are 4,0,4; population variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.667 and SD ≈ 1.633.

blocks.question: Now treat 1,3,5 as a sample. What changes?
blocks.answer: Sample variance = 8/(3−1) = 4. Sample SD = 2. Range and mean are unchanged.
blocks.text: Now treat 1,3,5 as a sample. What changes? Answer: Sample variance = 8/(3−1) = 4. Sample SD = 2. Range and mean are unchanged.

blocks.question: If SD is 4 cm and each value is doubled then increased by 10 cm, what is the new SD?
blocks.answer: 8 cm. Doubling doubles SD; adding 10 changes location only.
blocks.text: If SD is 4 cm and each value is doubled then increased by 10 cm, what is the new SD? Answer: 8 cm. Doubling doubles SD; adding 10 changes location only.

A percentile describes a position in an ordered dataset. The 50th percentile is the median. A 90th percentile is a cutoff near the upper end, not “90% marks”.

blocks.alt: The course hand rule gives Q1 = 47, while spreadsheet interpolation gives Q1 = 49.75 for the same marks.
blocks.caption: The course hand rule gives Q1 = 47, while spreadsheet interpolation gives Q1 = 49.75 for the same marks.

blocks.text: What a percentile means

For the lecture’s hand-rule definition, a 100p percentile is a cutoff with at least 100p% of the observations at or below it and at least 100(1−p)% at or above it. Here p is a proportion: use 0.25 for the 25th percentile. Ties mean the percentages on either side need not be exactly 25% and 75%.
Method A: the lecture’s hand-calculation rule

First sort the observations. For an interior percentile, 0 < p < 1, calculate np. If np is not a whole number, round it UP and take the observation at that position. If np is a whole number, average the observations at positions np and np+1. At p = 0 use the minimum; at p = 1 use the maximum, rather than looking for a nonexistent next observation.
Method B: spreadsheet linear interpolation

Split the rank into whole part i and fractional part d. Start at ordered value x[i], then move fraction d of the gap to x[i+1]. If rank is an integer, just use that ordered value; at the maximum rank use the maximum.
For the 25th percentile, rank = 1 + 9×0.25 = 3.25. Position 3 has 47 and position 4 has 58. Move one quarter of the 11-mark gap: 47 + 0.25×11 = 49.75.
For the 90th percentile, rank = 1 + 9×0.9 = 9.1. Positions 9 and 10 have 70 and 79. The result is 70 + 0.1×9 = 70.9. It differs from the hand-rule 74.5 because the definitions differ.
Using a spreadsheet

With the ten raw marks in A1:A10, enter =PERCENTILE(A1:A10,0.25). This interpolation-based function gives 49.75. For 90th percentile, use 0.9 rather than 90. Use the method requested in the question; a spreadsheet result does not automatically check a calculation done with a different definition.
Do not mix percentile definitions within one calculation. State the rule you used. The two methods are both explicitly presented in the supplied lecture.

blocks.question: For sorted 10,20,30,40,50, find the 30th percentile using the hand rule.
blocks.answer: n×p = 5×0.3 = 1.5; round up to position 2, giving 20.
blocks.text: For sorted 10,20,30,40,50, find the 30th percentile using the hand rule. Answer: n×p = 5×0.3 = 1.5; round up to position 2, giving 20.

blocks.question: For the same values, find it using interpolation.
blocks.text: For the same values, find it using interpolation. Answer: Rank = 1 + 4×0.3 = 2.2. Result = 20 + 0.2×(30−20) = 22.

blocks.question: Does the 90th percentile mean a student answered 90% correctly?
blocks.answer: No. A percentile is a position relative to other observations. Percentage marks measure a fraction of the available marks.
blocks.text: Does the 90th percentile mean a student answered 90% correctly? Answer: No. A percentile is a position relative to other observations. Percentage marks measure a fraction of the available marks.

sections.title: Quartiles, IQR, five-number summaries and boxplots
sections.source: Lecture 3.5; boxplot extension from course overview objectives

blocks.text: Quartiles divide ordered data into roughly four parts. Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q2 is the median, and Q3 is the 75th percentile. The interquartile range describes the spread of the middle half.

blocks.alt: The hand-rule summary is minimum 35, Q1 47, median 63.5, Q3 68, maximum 79.
blocks.caption: The hand-rule summary is minimum 35, Q1 47, median 63.5, Q3 68, maximum 79.

blocks.text: Five numbers describe position and spread
Write the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum, in that order. Use one percentile convention throughout.

Using the lecture hand rule gives IQR = 68−47 = 21. The lecture later uses spreadsheet Q1 = 49.75, so its IQR is 68−49.75 = 18.25. The difference is a change of convention, not an arithmetic disagreement.
Why use IQR?

Range uses the two extremes. IQR uses the middle half, so it is more resistant to an extreme value. “Middle half” is approximate with small samples and ties. For skewed data or outliers, median and IQR often describe a typical case and spread better than mean and SD.
Read a boxplot

The box goes from Q1 to Q3. A line inside marks the median. A basic minimum-to-maximum boxplot uses whiskers at the minimum and maximum. A modified boxplot instead places whiskers at the most extreme observed values inside the fences and shows flagged values as separate points. Always check which version is used.
An extra tool: 1.5 × IQR outlier fences

A value strictly below the lower fence or above the upper fence is flagged as a potential outlier. A fence is a cutoff, not necessarily an observed value or a whisker endpoint. A flag asks you to investigate; it is not permission to delete data automatically.

With hand-rule Q1 = 47 and Q3 = 68, IQR = 21. Fences are 15.5 and 99.5. All ten marks lie inside, so none are flagged by this rule. If an additional value is added, recompute the quartiles and fences for the new dataset.

Another worked example: take 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,30. The hand rule gives Q1 = (2+3)/2 = 2.5 and Q3 = (6+7)/2 = 6.5. IQR = 4. Fences are −3.5 and 12.5, so 30 is flagged. Modified whiskers reach 1 and 7, not the upper fence 12.5.

blocks.question: If Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32, find IQR and the fences.
blocks.answer: IQR = 12. Lower fence = 20−18 = 2. Upper fence = 32+18 = 50.
blocks.text: If Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32, find IQR and the fences. Answer: IQR = 12. Lower fence = 20−18 = 2. Upper fence = 32+18 = 50.

blocks.question: Using those fences, are 2,50,51 flagged?
blocks.answer: 2 and 50 are on the fences, so not flagged by the strict rule. 51 is above 50, so it is flagged.
blocks.text: Using those fences, are 2,50,51 flagged? Answer: 2 and 50 are on the fences, so not flagged by the strict rule. 51 is above 50, so it is flagged.

blocks.question: Does a larger IQR always mean a larger mean?
blocks.answer: No. IQR describes spread; mean describes location. A group can be widely spread around a small mean.
blocks.text: Does a larger IQR always mean a larger mean? Answer: No. IQR describes spread; mean describes location. A group can be widely spread around a small mean.

blocks.question: 1. Data: 2,2,3,4,4,4,5,6. Give a single-value frequency table.
blocks.text: 1. Data: 2,2,3,4,4,4,5,6. Give a single-value frequency table. Answer: 2:2, 3:1, 4:3, 5:1, 6:1. Total = 8. The share for 4 is 3/8 = 37.5%.

blocks.question: 2. For the same data, find mean, median and mode.
blocks.answer: Sum = 30, so mean = 30/8 = 3.75. Sorted middle values (positions 4 and 5) are both 4, so median = 4. Mode = 4 (3 times).

blocks.answer: Mean = 4. Squared deviations total 8. Population variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.667; SD ≈ 1.633.

blocks.question: 4. For sample 2,4,6, find variance and SD.
blocks.answer: Use n−1 = 2: sample variance = 8/2 = 4 and SD = 2.
blocks.text: 4. For sample 2,4,6, find variance and SD. Answer: Use n−1 = 2: sample variance = 8/2 = 4 and SD = 2.

blocks.question: 5. A dataset has mean 20, variance 9 and SD 3. Each value becomes 5−2x. Give the new summaries.
blocks.text: 5. A dataset has mean 20, variance 9 and SD 3. Each value becomes 5−2x. Give the new summaries. Answer: Mean = 5−2×20 = −35. Variance = (−2)²×9 = 36. SD = |−2|×3 = 6.

blocks.question: 6. Sorted data are 10,20,30,40,50,60. Find the 25th percentile by the hand rule.
blocks.answer: np = 6×0.25 = 1.5. Round up to position 2: percentile = 20.
blocks.text: 6. Sorted data are 10,20,30,40,50,60. Find the 25th percentile by the hand rule. Answer: np = 6×0.25 = 1.5. Round up to position 2: percentile = 20.

blocks.question: 7. Use spreadsheet interpolation for the same percentile.
blocks.text: 7. Use spreadsheet interpolation for the same percentile. Answer: Rank = 1 + 5×0.25 = 2.25. Interpolate: 20 + 0.25×(30−20) = 22.5.

blocks.question: 8. Q1 = 15, Q3 = 25. Find IQR, fences and whether 41 is flagged.
blocks.answer: IQR = 10. Fences = 0 and 40. Since 41 > 40, it is a potential outlier.
blocks.text: 8. Q1 = 15, Q3 = 25. Find IQR, fences and whether 41 is flagged. Answer: IQR = 10. Fences = 0 and 40. Since 41 > 40, it is a potential outlier.

blocks.question: 9. A class [20,30) contains a measurement of 30. Is that right?
blocks.answer: No. Under the left-in, right-out rule, 30 belongs to [30,40).
blocks.text: 9. A class [20,30) contains a measurement of 30. Is that right? Answer: No. Under the left-in, right-out rule, 30 belongs to [30,40).

blocks.question: 10. With key 3 | 4 = 34, interpret 5 | 0 1 1 8.
blocks.answer: 50,51,51,58. The repeated 1 preserves the repeated value 51.
blocks.text: 10. With key 3 | 4 = 34, interpret 5 | 0 1 1 8. Answer: 50,51,51,58. The repeated 1 preserves the repeated value 51.

blocks.question: 11. Two bins have widths 5 and 10, with frequencies 10 each. Give frequency densities.
blocks.answer: 10/5 = 2 and 10/10 = 1. Their bar areas are both 10.
blocks.text: 11. Two bins have widths 5 and 10, with frequencies 10 each. Give frequency densities. Answer: 10/5 = 2 and 10/10 = 1. Their bar areas are both 10.

blocks.question: 12. A group mean is 10 for 2 students, and another mean is 20 for 8 students. Find the combined mean.
blocks.answer: (2×10 + 8×20)/(2+8) = 180/10 = 18. Averaging group means without group sizes would give the wrong result 15.
